Every host knows the ritual: a guest asks for the Wi-Fi password, you recite a string of random letters and numbers, they mistype it twice, and you both stand there spelling it out character by character. A Wi-Fi QR code ends that ritual. Guests point their phone camera at one printed code and join instantly — no typing, no mistakes, no password dictated across the room.

## Make your free Wi-Fi QR code in 4 steps

You need three things: your network name (SSID), your Wi-Fi password, and the security type your router uses. All three are usually on a sticker on the router itself, or in your router's settings page.

1. Open the [free QR code generator](/tools/qr-code-generator) and choose the Wi-Fi content type.
2. Type in your network name, pick the security type that matches your router, and enter your Wi-Fi password.
3. Check the live preview, then download the code as a high-resolution PNG for printing (up to 2048 px) or as SVG if you want it razor-sharp at any size.
4. Test-scan it with your own phone before you print or share it — a 10-second check that saves an awkward moment later.

The code is generated entirely in your browser, so your Wi-Fi password is never uploaded or stored anywhere. And because the network details are encoded directly in the image, the code never expires — it keeps working until you change your network name or password.

## Where a Wi-Fi QR code actually helps

**At home.** Print one and stick it inside a kitchen cupboard or frame it near the entrance. Guests help themselves instead of asking, and you never have to remember whether your password has a zero or an O in it.

**In a cafe, salon, or small shop.** A code on the counter or on each table means customers connect in seconds and staff stop repeating the password all day. Print it at 1024 px or larger so it scans from a comfortable distance, not just at arm's length.

**In a rental or Airbnb.** Put the code in the welcome book or on the fridge. Guests arrive, scan, and are online before they have unpacked — one less message for you to answer.

**In an office or classroom.** A code on the meeting-room wall gets visitors and new starters on the guest network without anyone sharing the password out loud in front of the whole room.

## Printing tips that keep the code scannable

A QR code that does not scan is worse than no code at all, so a few details matter. Keep the dark-on-light contrast strong — fancy low-contrast colors look good and scan badly, and the generator warns you if your color pair is too weak. Leave the quiet zone, the blank margin around the code, intact; scanners need that empty border to find the code. And keep the code reasonably large: a tiny code on a busy menu forces people to hold their phone inches away, while a palm-sized code scans from a normal distance.

If you add a logo to the center of the code, keep it at the default size. The generator automatically raises the error correction to at least Medium when a logo is present, so the covered modules can still be recovered — but a giant logo over a dense code is asking for trouble.

## The honest security note

A Wi-Fi QR code is exactly as secure as telling someone your password — because that is what it does. Anyone who photographs the code can decode it and read the password, so treat a printed code the way you would treat the password itself. For guests, the clean solution is a separate guest network: most modern routers offer one in a few clicks, and then the code you hand out only opens the guest network, never your main one with your laptops, printers, and smart-home devices on it.

Also remember that the code is a snapshot, not a live link. Change your Wi-Fi password and every printed code stops working until you generate a fresh one. That is a feature as much as a limitation: when you rotate a guest password, old codes die with it.

## What if a guest's phone won't scan it?

First, check the obvious: is the camera app's QR scanning switched on, and is the code well lit and in focus? On most modern iPhones and Android phones, the built-in camera app reads QR codes with no extra app needed — point, wait for the prompt, tap to join. If scanning still fails, re-check the details you typed: a single wrong character in the network name or password produces a perfectly good-looking code that joins nothing. Regenerate after fixing the typo, and test-scan again before reprinting.

For the reverse problem — a QR code someone sent you that you need to read — the [free QR code scanner](/tools/qr-scanner) decodes codes from a saved photo or screenshot right in your browser, no app install needed.
